evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two complexes.

claim: The RR REC domain adopts a unique conformation in both phosphatase and phosphotransferase complexes, with an average rmsd of 0.3 Å aligning all Cα atoms.
source: On the other hand, the RR REC domain adopts a unique conformation in both complexes, with an average rmsd of 0.3 Å aligning all Cα atoms, and no significant contrast clustering phosphatase vs phosphotransferase structures (Table 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and analysis.

claim: The conformation adopted by the REC domain in complex with the kinase combines structural features of both active and inactive states as seen in the free forms of RRs.
source: Interestingly, this conformation adopted by the REC domain in complex with the kinase, combines structural features of both active and inactive states as seen in the free forms of RRs (Gao and Stock, 2009; Trajtenberg et al., 2014) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with cited prior work.

claim: The β4α4 loop and β5 strand in the complexed REC emulate the inactive RR, while the rest of the protein resembles the free phosphorylated species.
source: Namely, the β4α4 loop and β5 strand emulate the inactive RR, while the rest of the protein resembles the free phosphorylated species.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the complexed and free RR structures.

claim: The β4α4 loop is closed in phosphorylated RRs, coupled to a fully wound first turn of helix α4.
source: The β4α4 loop is closed in phosphorylated RRs (e.g. PDB 4LE0), coupled to a fully wound first turn of helix α4 (Pro85(RR) displays a dihedral ψ angle near −40°, allowing for α-helicity).
evidence: This is a structural observation from prior work on phosphorylated RRs.

claim: The REC molecules in both phosphatase and phosphotransferase complexes show the β4α4 loop open with Pro85(RR) ψ angles of respectively 126° and 130°, and the first turn of α4 unwound, as observed in the inactive state.
source: The REC molecules in both phosphatase and phosphotransferase complexes, show instead this β4α4 loop open (with Pro85(RR) ψ angles of respectively 126° and 130°, and the first turn of α4 unwound, as observed in the inactive state of the Mg2+-free protein [PDB 4LE1]).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures.

claim: The β4α4 loop acts as a 'phosphate lid', opening and closing to control phosphoryl-transfer chemistry on Asp54(RR).
source: Thus acting as a 'phosphate lid', the β4α4 loop opens and closes to control phosphoryl-transfer chemistry on Asp54(RR) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: HK-binding triggers RR 'activation', as predicted based on functional readouts and in silico modeling.
source: Regarding the positions of the phosphorylatable Asp, as well those of the β1α1 loop and contiguous helix α1, HK-binding triggers RR 'activation', as we had previously predicted based on functional readouts and in silico modeling (Trajtenberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and prior predictions cited.

claim: The shift of loop β1α1 locates key acidic residues in place to coordinate the essential Mg2+ cation within the RR's reaction center.
source: The shift of loop β1α1 locates key acidic residues in place to coordinate the essential Mg2+ cation within the RR's reaction center.
evidence: This is a structural observation with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The RR adopts a single intermediate pre-activated conformation, instrumental for both dephosphorylation and phosphotransfer reactions.
source: Taken together, the RR adopts a single intermediate pre-activated conformation, instrumental for both dephosphorylation and phosphotransfer reactions, due to increased exposure of the phosphorylation site and stabilized configuration of the pocket poised for reaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The crystal structure of wt P~DesKC was determined, improving previous resolution limits.
source: The crystal structure of wt P~DesKC was determined (Table 1), improving previous resolution limits (Albanesi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on crystallographic data.

claim: The reactive His188(HK) was observed to be phosphorylated on its Nε2 atom in wt P~DesKC.
source: The reactive His188(HK) was observed to be phosphorylated on its Nε2 atom (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and superposition of this model onto the HK partner of the phosphotransferase complex (PDB 5IUK) revealed very similar structures, with 1.2 Å rmsd aligning all 1994 atoms that comprise the DHp domain and the fixed CA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: Superposition of wt P~DesKC onto the HK partner of the phosphotransferase complex revealed very similar structures, with 1.2 Å rmsd aligning all 1994 atoms that comprise the DHp domain and the fixed CA.
source: The reactive His188(HK) was observed to be phosphorylated on its Nε2 atom (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and superposition of this model onto the HK partner of the phosphotransferase complex (PDB 5IUK) revealed very similar structures, with 1.2 Å rmsd aligning all 1994 atoms that comprise the DHp domain and the fixed CA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Substituting the DesKCH188E component in the crystal complex by the superposed wt P~DesKC revealed surprisingly good geometry between P~DesKC and DesR-REC.
source: Substituting the DesKCH188E component in the crystal complex by the superposed wt P~DesKC, revealed surprisingly good geometry between P~DesKC and DesR-REC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling.

claim: Energy minimization easily fixed minor interatomic bumping, rendering a model with P~His188(HK) well oriented toward Asp54(RR), poised for phosphotransfer.
source: Energy minimization easily fixed minor interatomic bumping, rendering a model with P~His188(HK) well oriented toward Asp54(RR), poised for phosphotransfer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling.

claim: The P~His188(HK)Nε2, phosphorus and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 atoms describe a~180° angle in the phosphotransferase model.
source: The P~His188(HK)Nε2, phosphorus and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 atoms describe a~180° angle, with the phosphoryl group at H-bonding distance to the side chain oxygens of Thr80(RR) and Thr81(RR).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The phosphoryl group is at H-bonding distance to the side chain oxygens of Thr80(RR) and Thr81(RR) in the phosphotransferase model.
source: The P~His188(HK)Nε2, phosphorus and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 atoms describe a~180° angle, with the phosphoryl group at H-bonding distance to the side chain oxygens of Thr80(RR) and Thr81(RR).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The wt P~DesKC:DesR-REC model proved to be stable in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The model proved to be stable in molecular dynamics simulations (Figure 4B), overall making chemical and biological sense.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: An ~80° rotation of helix α1 is coupled to a cogwheel-like shift of helix α2 at the level of the phosphorylation site within the DHp domain during the phosphatase→phosphotransferase switch.
source: The phosphatase→phosphotransferase switch engages major rearrangements. An ~80° rotation of helix α1 is coupled to a cogwheel-like shift of helix α2, at the level of the phosphorylation site within the DHp domain (Albanesi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The rotation during the phosphatase→phosphotransferase switch includes the phosphorylatable His188(HK), which had not been previously observed.
source: This rotation includes the phosphorylatable His188(HK) (Figure 4C), which had not been previously observed.
evidence: This is a new structural observation from the current study.

claim: The side chain of His188(HK) ends up buried in the phosphatase state, establishing a H-bond with the same residue of the other protomer.
source: Due to this shift, the side chain of His188(HK) ends up buried in the phosphatase state, establishing a H-bond with the same residue of the other protomer (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), displaced away from the reaction center as compared to the phosphotransferase (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: His188(HK) is displaced away from the reaction center in the phosphatase state as compared to the phosphotransferase.
source: Due to this shift, the side chain of His188(HK) ends up buried in the phosphatase state, establishing a H-bond with the same residue of the other protomer (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), displaced away from the reaction center as compared to the phosphotransferase (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two complexes.

claim: Asp189(HK) undergoes a dramatic rearrangement, well positioned only in the phosphatase complex to make a salt bridge with Arg84(RR).
source: Asp189(HK) right next to the phosphorylation site, follows a similarly dramatic rearrangement, well positioned only in the phosphatase complex to make a salt bridge with Arg84(RR).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures.

claim: Phe82(RR) inserts its aromatic side chain into a hydrophobic pocket formed between DHp α1 of one HK protomer and α2' of the other in the phosphatase complex.
source: Neighboring Phe82(RR) thus inserts its aromatic side chain into a hydrophobic pocket formed between DHp α1 of one HK protomer and α2' of the other (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The reactive histidine moving away from the catalytic site in the phosphatase state is consistent with its marginal role in P~RR dephosphorylation catalysis in HisKA_3 HKs.
source: That the reactive histidine moves away from the catalytic site in the phosphatase state is consistent with its marginal role in P~RR dephosphorylation catalysis in HisKA_3 HKs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: The phosphorylatable His was proved nonessential for NarX-mediated P~NarL dephosphorylation.
source: Indeed, the phosphorylatable His was proved nonessential for NarX-mediated P~NarL dephosphorylation (Huynh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: His has been implicated in EnvZ-mediated phosphatase catalysis, in which case its imidazole would act as a base assisting the attack of water on the P~aspartyl group.
source: His has been implicated in EnvZ-mediated phosphatase catalysis (Zhu et al., 2000) in which case its imidazole would act as a base assisting the attack of water on the P~aspartyl group (Bhate et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Contradictory results cast doubts on the direct role of His in phosphatase catalysis.
source: But contradictory results cast doubts on such a direct role (Hsing and Silhavy, 1997; Skarphol et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A Gln in HisKA_3, corresponding to Gln193(HK) in DesK, plays a key role in the phosphatase reaction, positioning a catalytic water molecule.
source: Instead, a Gln in HisKA_3 (Huynh et al., 2010), corresponding to Gln193(HK) in DesK, or a Thr/Asn in HisKA HKs (Willett and Kirby, 2012), equivalently positioned one helical turn C-terminal to the phosphorylatable His, play a key role in the phosphatase reaction, positioning a catalytic water molecule.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A Thr/Asn in HisKA HKs, equivalently positioned one helical turn C-terminal to the phosphorylatable His, plays a key role in the phosphatase reaction, positioning a catalytic water molecule.
source: Instead, a Gln in HisKA_3 (Huynh et al., 2010), corresponding to Gln193(HK) in DesK, or a Thr/Asn in HisKA HKs (Willett and Kirby, 2012), equivalently positioned one helical turn C-terminal to the phosphorylatable His, play a key role in the phosphatase reaction, positioning a catalytic water molecule.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The catalytic water or hydroxide molecule is well located to perform the nucleophilic attack on the phosphoryl group, as observed in the P~CheY3 phosphatase CheX.
source: Such water or hydroxide molecule is well located to perform the nucleophilic attack on the phosphoryl group, as observed in the P~CheY3 phosphatase CheX (Pazy et al., 2010), a shared geometry among phosphatases and HKs as we now observe in the DesKC:DesR-REC phosphatase complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and structural observation.

claim: The rotational phosphatase→phosphotransferase rearrangement disrupts the Asp189(HK):Arg84(RR) ionic bond.
source: The rotational phosphatase→phosphotransferase rearrangement disrupts the Asp189(HK):Arg84(RR) ionic bond, and coupled to the α1(HK) and α2'(HK) movements, the position of Phe82(RR) shifts, propagating along the rest of the phosphate lid β4α4 loop (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two complexes.

claim: The shift of Phe82(RR) propagates along the rest of the phosphate lid β4α4 loop.
source: The rotational phosphatase→phosphotransferase rearrangement disrupts the Asp189(HK):Arg84(RR) ionic bond, and coupled to the α1(HK) and α2'(HK) movements, the position of Phe82(RR) shifts, propagating along the rest of the phosphate lid β4α4 loop (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two complexes.

claim: The shift of Phe82(RR) accounts for the capacity of Thr80(RR) to be at H-bonding distance from the P~His188(HK) phosphoryl moiety, accompanying its transfer, and maintaining the H-bond to the phosphate on P~Asp54(RR).
source: This shift accounts for the capacity of Thr80(RR) to be at H-bonding distance from the P~His188(HK) phosphoryl moiety, accompanying its transfer, and maintaining the H-bond to the phosphate on P~Asp54(RR) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: The side chain of Phe82(RR) is contacting P~His188(HK), which could increase the pKa of its imidazole Nδ1 atom due to cation-π interactions.
source: The side chain of Phe82(RR) is also contacting P~His188(HK), which could increase the pKa of its imidazole Nδ1 atom due to cation-π interactions (Loewenthal et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observation and cited prior work.

claim: P~DesKC appeared to catalyze slower phosphoryl-transfer to DesR-RECF82A compared to wt DesR-REC.
source: Indeed, P~DesKC appeared to catalyze slower phosphoryl-transfer to DesR-RECF82A compared to wt DesR-REC (Figure 4E), consistent with a poorer Nδ1 protonation, and hence a stronger P-N phosphoramidate bond (Attwood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The phosphatase and phosphotransferase catalytic activities depend upon modifications in the position of a subset of residues in both partners.
source: Thus, the phosphatase and phosphotransferase catalytic activities depend upon modifications in the position of a subset of residues in both partners.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: Both phosphatase and phosphotransferase complexes share a common RR intermediate conformation, and the reaction outcome is dictated by the HK switch of helices α1 and α2.
source: Both complexes share a common RR intermediate conformation, and the reaction outcome is dictated by the HK switch of helices α1 and α2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: DesK:DesR-catalyzed phosphotransfer occurred essentially in the forward, P~DesK→DesR direction.
source: DesK:DesR-catalyzed phosphotransfer occurred essentially in the forward, P~DesK→DesR direction (Figure 5A), extending earlier suggestions (Albanesi et al., 2004) into quantitative figures, and indicating that back-transfer is minimal.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: Back-transfer in the DesK:DesR system is minimal.
source: DesK:DesR-catalyzed phosphotransfer occurred essentially in the forward, P~DesK→DesR direction (Figure 5A), extending earlier suggestions (Albanesi et al., 2004) into quantitative figures, and indicating that back-transfer is minimal.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The side chain of Thr80(RR) at the end of β4 strand appears to drive the whole phosphate lid to a closed configuration, escorting the phosphoryl group during P~His→Asp migration.
source: The side chain of Thr80(RR) at the end of β4 strand, appears to drive the whole phosphate lid to a closed configuration, escorting the phosphoryl group during P~His→Asp migration (Figures 3 and 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Phe82(RR) was substituted by alanine to test whether a closed phosphate lid plays a role in minimizing P~RR dephosphorylation.
source: To test whether a closed phosphate lid indeed plays a role in minimizing P~RR dephosphorylation, as a means to ensuring phosphotransfer unidirectionality, Phe82(RR) was substituted by alanine.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Phe82(RR) covers the P~Asp54(RR) in active free DesR, while exposing it to bulk solvent through phosphate lid-opening when bound to DesK.
source: Phe82(RR) covers the P~Asp54(RR) in active free DesR, while exposing it to bulk solvent through phosphate lid-opening when bound to DesK (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The half-life of P~DesRF82A was significantly reduced when compared to wt P~DesR.
source: The half-life of P~DesRF82A was significantly reduced when compared to wt P~DesR (Figure 5B), confirming that the phosphate lid is a key structural element to avoid otherwise futile P~RR dephosphorylation after phosphotransfer.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The phosphate lid is a key structural element to avoid futile P~RR dephosphorylation after phosphotransfer.
source: The half-life of P~DesRF82A was significantly reduced when compared to wt P~DesR (Figure 5B), confirming that the phosphate lid is a key structural element to avoid otherwise futile P~RR dephosphorylation after phosphotransfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The distance between P~His188(HK)Nε2 and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 in the phosphotransferase complex is ~7.6 Å.
source: The distance between P~His188(HK)Nε2 and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 in the phosphotransferase complex is ~7.6 Å (Figures 4A and 5C), strongly suggesting that the phosphotransfer reaction occurs through a loose (or predominantly dissociative) nucleophilic substitution mechanism.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the model.

claim: The phosphotransfer reaction in DesK:DesR occurs through a loose (or predominantly dissociative) nucleophilic substitution mechanism.
source: The distance between P~His188(HK)Nε2 and Asp54(RR)Oδ1 in the phosphotransferase complex is ~7.6 Å (Figures 4A and 5C), strongly suggesting that the phosphotransfer reaction occurs through a loose (or predominantly dissociative) nucleophilic substitution mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural measurement.

claim: Reversible complexes efficiently catalyze phosphotransfer also in the opposite, P~Asp→His direction and display significantly shorter Nε2-to-Oδ1 distances, consistent with an associative nucleophilic mechanism.
source: This is in contrast to what has been observed in reversible complexes (Figure 5C), which efficiently catalyze phosphotransfer also in the opposite, P~Asp→His direction. The latter display significantly shorter Nε2-to-Oδ1 distances, consistent with an associative nucleophilic mechanism (Table 6).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other complexes.

claim: Examples of reversible complexes include several phosphorelay protein pairs and E. coli CheY variants in complex with imidazole.
source: Examples include several phosphorelay protein pairs (Bauer et al., 2013; Zapf et al., 2000; Zhao et al., 2008) as well as Escherichia coli CheY variants in complex with imidazole (Page et al., 2015), or yet two autophosphorylating HKs where the phosphoryl group is poised to migrate from ATP to the reactive histidine (Casino et al., 2014; Mechaly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HK:RR TCSs with unidirectional P~His→Asp transfer, such as B. subtilis DesK:DesR, T. maritima HK853:RR469 and R. sphaeroides CheA3:CheY6, consistently show >6.6 Å HisNε2-AspOδ1 distances.
source: In contrast, HK:RR TCSs with unidirectional P~His→Asp transfer, such as B. subtilis DesK:DesR (this study), Thermotoga maritima HK853:RR469 (Casino et al., 2009) and Rhodobacter sphaeroides CheA3:CheY6 (Bell et al., 2010), consistently show >6.6 Å HisNε2-AspOδ1 distances and correlated large reaction coordinate distances when these could be measured (Table 6).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with cited prior work.

claim: In a loose reaction center like that of DesK:DesR, a largely dissociated meta-phosphate intermediate would be stabilized migrating toward the positive charges of the Mg2+ cation and the conserved Lys102(RR) in the RR partner.
source: In a loose reaction center like that of DesK:DesR, a largely dissociated meta-phosphate intermediate would be stabilized migrating toward the positive charges of the Mg2+ cation and the conserved Lys102(RR) in the RR partner.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The position of the Mg2+ cation and Lys102(RR) next to the RR phosphorylation site introduces an intrinsic asymmetry within the reaction center, which translates into unequal likelihood for phosphoryl-transfer directions.
source: The position of these positive charges, next to the RR phosphorylation site, introduces an intrinsic asymmetry within the reaction center, which must translate into unequal likelihood for phosphoryl-transfer directions.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: As the Mg2+ position becomes more asymmetric, the P~Asp→His back-transfer would be less favorable, explaining unidirectionality.
source: As the Mg2+ position becomes more asymmetric, the P~Asp→His back-transfer would be less favorable, explaining unidirectionality.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The ratio between the Mg2+-Asp(Oδ1) and the Mg2+-His(Nε2) distances can be used to quantitate asymmetry within reaction centers.
source: The ratio between the Mg2+-Asp(Oδ1) and the Mg2+-His(Nε2) distances, can be used to quantitate such asymmetry within reaction centers.
evidence: This describes a metric used for analysis.

claim: The Mg2+ asymmetry ratio clusters complexes that catalyze reversible P~Asp→His/P~His→Asp reactions apart from ones that carry out P~His→Asp unidirectional transfer.
source: This ratio was calculated for different TCS complexes (Table 6), indeed clustering those complexes that catalyze reversible P~Asp→His/P~His→Asp reactions, apart from the ones that carry out P~His→Asp unidirectional transfer (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of multiple structures.

claim: Signaling pathways have evolved associative or dissociative mechanisms, corresponding respectively to more reversible or irreversible reactions, such that they are fit to drive a defined directionality in the flow of information.
source: Signaling pathways appear to have evolved associative or dissociative mechanisms, corresponding respectively to more reversible or irreversible reactions, such that they are fit to drive a defined directionality in the flow of information.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion based on comparative structural analysis.

claim: The small number of interactions and low surface complementarity in the DesKC:DesR complexes are consistent with the observed 'slippery' nature of the protein:protein interface.
source: The small number of interactions and low surface complementarity that we observe in the several DesKC:DesR complexes (Figure 2F) are consistent with the observed 'slippery' nature of the protein:protein interface, displaying significant shifts in the relative positions of both partners.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphotransferase complex recapitulated the gliding shifts of one partner with respect to the other, reaching the different arrangements observed in the crystal structures at different moments of the simulations.
source: Further supporting that this ensemble of conformations is functionally relevant, molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphotransferase complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) recapitulated the gliding shifts of one partner with respect to the other, reaching the different arrangements observed in the crystal structures at different moments of the simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Loose HK:RR association architectures can be observed in other TCS-related complexes, suggesting it is a universal feature.
source: Loose HK:RR association architectures can actually be observed in other TCS-related complexes (Zapf et al., 2000; Casino et al., 2009; Willett et al., 2015), suggesting it is a universal feature.
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited prior work.

claim: Loose HK:RR interfaces explain the considerable promiscuity reported in different TCSs in in vitro assays.
source: This explains the considerable promiscuity reported in different TCSs in in vitro assays, if long enough incubation times are allowed for a given HK to phosphotransfer to different RRs, including surrogate partners (Skerker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations and cited prior work.

claim: HK:RR interactions ensure high specificity, but also avoid exceedingly high stability, which would hinder proper functional modulation and signal transmission.
source: HK:RR interactions thus ensure high specificity, but also avoiding exceedingly high stability, which would hinder proper functional modulation and, ultimately, signal transmission altogether.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Loose, slippery interfaces are inherently tolerant for substantial sequence variation of protein:protein contacting residues.
source: Evolutionarily selected to be loose, slippery interfaces are inherently tolerant for substantial sequence variation of protein:protein contacting residues.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: The tolerance for sequence variation is consistent with the extensive degeneracy found in TCS pairs, likely a general feature of HK:RR interactions.
source: Such tolerance is consistent with the extensive degeneracy found in TCS pairs (Podgornaia and Laub, 2015), likely a general feature of HK:RR interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Epistasis is a key property of HK:RR interfaces.
source: The DesK:DesR structures now provide with molecular details explaining why epistasis is found as a key property of HK:RR interfaces (Podgornaia and Laub, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and structural data.

claim: Epistatic amino acid changes depend on the presence of other substitutions, leading to different effects in combination than individually.
source: Epistatic amino acid changes are those that depend on the presence of other substitutions, leading to different effects in combination than individually.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge.

claim: Interfacing residue replacements on any one of the TCS components can easily be accommodated due to the loose character of the protein:protein association.
source: While interfacing residue replacements on any one of the TCS components can easily be accommodated due to the loose character of the protein:protein association, epistatic substitutions in the same component and/or in the other partner, are called to play essential stabilizing or destabilizing compensatory roles.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Epistatic substitutions play essential stabilizing or destabilizing compensatory roles in HK:RR interfaces.
source: While interfacing residue replacements on any one of the TCS components can easily be accommodated due to the loose character of the protein:protein association, epistatic substitutions in the same component and/or in the other partner, are called to play essential stabilizing or destabilizing compensatory roles.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Epistatic substitutions are selected such that partner recognition and non-cognate discrimination are maintained, but without leading to overstable, non-functional complexes.
source: Epistatic substitutions are thus selected, such that partner recognition and non-cognate discrimination are maintained, but without leading to overstable, non-functional complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The HK is largely unable to discriminate binding to RR or P~RR on the basis of structural determinants.
source: Our data indicate that the HK is largely unable to discriminate binding to RR or P~RR on the basis of structural determinants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claim: The two complexes show equivalent HK:RR interfacing surfaces, with all major contacts preserved.
source: The two complexes also show equivalent HK:RR interfacing surfaces, with all major contacts preserved.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two complexes.

claim: Among the few differential contacts between phosphatase and phosphotransferase complexes, they mainly implicate the HK's CA domain, but are unlikely to grant discrimination ability.
source: Among the few differential contacts, they mainly implicate the HK's CA domain, but unlikely to grant discrimination ability given the highly similar conformation of the RR in those regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Calorimetry data reveal only modest differences between DesR-REC:DesKCH188V and DesR-REC:DesKCH188E binding affinities.
source: Calorimetry data are consistent with the crystallographic evidence, revealing only modest differences between DesR-REC:DesKCH188Vand DesR-REC:DesKCH188E binding affinities (Figure 1 and Table 2), further supporting that both HK functional states interact with DesR-REC with similar strengths.
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data.

claim: Both HK functional states interact with DesR-REC with similar strengths.
source: Calorimetry data are consistent with the crystallographic evidence, revealing only modest differences between DesR-REC:DesKCH188Vand DesR-REC:DesKCH188E binding affinities (Figure 1 and Table 2), further supporting that both HK functional states interact with DesR-REC with similar strengths.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on ITC data.

claim: EnvZ binds OmpR and P~OmpR with equivalent affinities.
source: EnvZ binds OmpR and P~OmpR with equivalent affinities (Yoshida et al., 2002), as well as PhoQ binding to PhoP or P~PhoP (Castelli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PhoQ binds to PhoP or P~PhoP with equivalent affinities.
source: EnvZ binds OmpR and P~OmpR with equivalent affinities (Yoshida et al., 2002), as well as PhoQ binding to PhoP or P~PhoP (Castelli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When the pathway is turned off, HK autophosphorylation is inhibited by hindering CA domains mobility and DHp helical rotation.
source: When the pathway is turned off, HK autophosphorylation is inhibited by: 1) hindering CA domains mobility, holding ATP substrates far from the His188(HK) phosphorylation site; and, 2) DHp helical rotation, making the His188(HK) side chains inaccessible (Figures 4D and 6A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on structural observations.

claim: The 'open' autokinase-off configuration is linked to a folded N-terminal coiled-coil, in which DesK can bind P~DesR and trigger phosphatase catalysis.
source: This 'open' autokinase-off configuration is linked to a folded N-terminal coiled-coil, in which DesK can bind P~DesR and trigger phosphatase catalysis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on structural observations.

claim: Linked to P~DesR phosphate lid opening, Asp189(HK) binds to Arg84(RR), and Phe82(RR) becomes inserted into a DHp pocket.
source: Linked to P~DesR phosphate lid opening, Asp189(HK) binds to Arg84(RR), and Phe82(RR) becomes inserted into a DHp pocket (Figure 6A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on structural observations.

claim: Phe82(RR) removal from the closed position allows an incoming nucleophilic water molecule to bring about dephosphorylation.
source: Phe82(RR) is thus removed from the closed position, which would otherwise clash with an incoming nucleophilic water molecule (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) that brings about dephosphorylation (Pazy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on structural observations and cited prior work.

claim: DesK Gln193(HK) is well located to position the catalytic water to perform dephosphorylation.
